title: Natural Environment
summary: ## Ecosystem and its components

An ecosystem is all the organisms living in an area together with the non-living physical surroundings with which they interact (concept by A.G. Tansley, 1935; Greek oikos, home). Natural ecosystems are terrestrial (grassland, desert, forest) or aquatic (pond, river, ocean); artificial ones are gardens, aquaria and crop fields. Abiotic components are the non-living physical and chemical factors — sunlight, temperature, precipitation, water, soil, air, minerals. Biotic components are the living organisms — producers, herbivores, carnivores, omnivores and decomposers (detritivores). Abiotic factors decide which organisms can live in a place (coastal, hill and desert plants differ).
## Biotic community

A biotic community is the populations of different organisms sharing a habitat. By mode of nutrition: autotrophs (producers) make their own food by photosynthesis (green plants; phytoplankton and macrophytes in water) or chemosynthesis (some bacteria) and form the base of every ecosystem; heterotrophs (consumers) feed on others — herbivores are primary consumers, carnivores secondary and tertiary consumers; saprotrophs (decomposers — bacteria and fungi) break down dead organic matter into simple substances and return them to the environment, linking living and non-living parts. A pond has abiotic parts (water, dissolved O₂ and CO₂, minerals, soil) and biotic parts (phytoplankton, plants, zooplankton, fish, decomposers); its top, middle and bottom layers differ in light, temperature and oxygen.
## Food chains and food webs

A food chain is a sequence of organisms through which food energy passes as each eats the one below it: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk; phytoplankton → small fish → large fish. Each step is a trophic level — producers I, herbivores II, carnivores III and so on. A grazing food chain starts from green plants; a detritus food chain starts from dead organic matter broken down by bacteria and fungi, whose products and bodies feed small animals and then larger carnivores — it recycles nutrients. Interconnected food chains form a food web. Significance: food chains and webs maintain ecological balance, show feeding relationships, and are the routes of energy flow and nutrient cycling; removing one species upsets the balance.
## Energy flow

The sun is the source of energy for all ecosystems. Energy flows in one direction only — from producers to herbivores to carnivores — and never returns. At each level only a small part (about 10%) of the energy becomes new body mass; the rest is lost as heat or used in life processes such as respiration and movement. So energy decreases at each higher trophic level, a carnivore must eat many herbivores, and food chains rarely have more than four or five levels.
## Biogeochemical cycles

Nutrients (carbon, nitrogen, water, oxygen, phosphorus, sulphur) are never lost; they cycle between the living and non-living parts — unlike energy flow, these cycles are circular. Carbon cycle: carbon is exchanged among living things, soil, water and air — plants take in CO₂ in photosynthesis; respiration, decay and burning of fuels return it; deforestation and burning fossil fuels add excess CO₂.

Nitrogen cycle (atmospheric nitrogen, 78% of air, is the biggest source; nitrogen is needed for proteins and nucleic acids): (1) Nitrogen fixation — conversion of atmospheric nitrogen into usable compounds, by lightning (N₂ and O₂ form oxides that dissolve in rain) and by free-living microbes (blue-green algae) and symbiotic Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules of legumes; (2) Assimilation — plants absorb nitrates to make amino acids and proteins; animals get them by eating plants; (3) Ammonification — urea, excreta and dead bodies are converted into ammonia by ammonifying bacteria; (4) Nitrification — nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter) convert ammonia into nitrites and nitrates; (5) Denitrification — bacteria such as Pseudomonas convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas. Water cycle: evaporation, condensation, precipitation and run-off move the limited water between components.
## Ecosystem services
Ecosystems give us oxygen, food, water, wood, fuel and minerals, regulate climate, control pests through predators, and recycle wastes — free of cost, so they must be used wisely.
## Adaptations

Adaptations are special features that let an organism live in a particular habitat. Hydrophytes (water plants — lotus, water lily, Hydrilla, Vallisneria, water hyacinth): reduced roots; floating leaves with stomata only on the upper surface and a waxy upper coating to repel water; thin, narrow or ribbon-shaped submerged leaves; long, spongy stems with air spaces (lotus) for buoyancy. Aquatic animals: streamlined bodies; fins for swimming, steering and balance; gills (fish, prawns); webbed feet (ducks); swim bladder for buoyancy; blubber (whales); eyes and nostrils on top of the head (frogs, crocodiles, whales).

Mesophytes (most land plants, moderate water): large, thin, broad leaves with many stomata on the lower surface; well-developed branched roots; well-organised shoots. Xerophytes (desert plants — cacti): succulent water-storing stems or leaves, few or no leaves or leaves turned into spines, fewer sunken stomata, thick waxy cuticle, deep spreading roots. Desert animals: stay in burrows by day and come out at night; scaly skin; reptiles excrete solid uric acid to save water; camels store fat in the hump, drink large amounts at once and pass concentrated urine. Cold-climate animals: thick fur, fat layer under the skin, rounded bodies with short ears and tails; penguins have densely packed feathers. Flying animals: streamlined body, forelimbs modified into wings (feathers in birds; in bats a skin extension between the fingers), hollow light bones, strong flight muscles.
## Population interactions

Mutualism benefits both partners — in lichens an alga makes food and a fungus gives water, minerals and shelter. Commensalism benefits one and does not affect the other — sucker fish on a shark, hermit crab in a snail shell. Parasitism benefits one and harms the host — tapeworm in human intestine. Symbiosis is any close living-together of two species (bees and flowers).
## Population growth

A population is a group of individuals of one species in an area. Its size depends on natality (births per thousand per unit time), mortality (deaths), and dispersal — emigration (permanent movement out, decreasing it) and immigration (movement in, increasing it). Environmental resistance (limited food, space, predators, disease) stops a population growing at its maximum rate; carrying capacity is the largest population the environment can sustain. Growth curves: S-shaped (sigmoid) — lag phase, rapid growth phase, then a stable phase when births equal deaths; J-shaped — exponential growth followed by a sudden crash when resistance takes effect.

vsa: Write two differences between grazing and detritus food chains.

A grazing food chain starts with living green plants, eaten by herbivores (grass → deer → lion); a detritus food chain starts with dead organic matter broken down by decomposers (dead leaves → bacteria/fungi → earthworm → bird). The grazing chain passes energy captured by photosynthesis; the detritus chain recycles nutrients from dead matter.

or: Write a grazing food chain with an example.
Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk (in water: phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → large fish).

vsa: Write two adaptations of desert animals that reduce water loss.
Any two: they excrete solid uric acid or concentrated urine; they have scaly, waterproof skin; they stay in burrows during the hot day and come out at night.
Why is energy less at higher trophic levels?
At each level most of the energy taken in is used for life processes (respiration, movement) or lost as heat; only about 10% becomes body mass and passes to the next level.
Why are detritus food chains important?
They break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil, so nutrients are recycled and the environment is kept clean.

or: Give two ways to replenish forests.
Afforestation/reforestation (planting trees where forests are cut) and social forestry or banning illegal felling and protecting forests from fire and grazing.

vsa: Name two adaptations of the lotus to live in water.
Long, spongy stem with air spaces that keeps it afloat and bends with currents; broad floating leaves with a waxy upper surface and stomata on the upper side.
Differentiate between emigration and immigration and state their effect on population size.
Emigration is permanent movement of individuals out of a population — it decreases the population. Immigration is permanent movement into a population — it increases it.
sa: What are mesophytes? Write two structural features.

Mesophytes are land plants that grow where water is neither very scarce nor in excess. Features: large, thin, broad leaves with many stomata on the lower surface; well-developed, branched roots with root caps; well-organised shoot system.

sa: What is symbiosis? Give an example. How is commensalism different from symbiosis (mutualism)?

Symbiosis is the close living together of two organisms of different species, e.g. alga and fungus in lichen, or bees and flowers. In mutualism both partners benefit; in commensalism one benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed (sucker fish on a shark).
October 2025
What is population dispersal? Describe its two types.

Dispersal is the movement of individuals into or out of an area, which changes the size of the population. Emigration is permanent movement out of a population (decreases it); immigration is permanent movement into a population (increases it).

Name two types of food chains and give two significances of food chains and food webs.

Grazing food chain (starts with green plants) and detritus food chain (starts with dead organic matter). Significance: they maintain ecological balance; they show feeding relationships; energy flows and nutrients cycle through them.

la: Draw a schematic diagram of the nitrogen cycle and explain the process.

Diagram: atmospheric N₂ → (lightning; nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules and soil) → nitrates in soil → absorbed by plants (proteins) → eaten by animals → excreta and dead bodies → ammonia (ammonifying bacteria) → nitrites and nitrates (nitrifying bacteria) → back to plants, or → N₂ (denitrifying bacteria). Steps: (1) nitrogen fixation by lightning and by microbes such as Rhizobium and blue-green algae; (2) assimilation of nitrates by plants into amino acids and proteins, passed to animals; (3) ammonification of urea, excreta and dead matter into ammonia; (4) nitrification — Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter convert ammonia into nitrites and nitrates; (5) denitrification — Pseudomonas returns nitrogen gas to the air.

la: What is an ecosystem? Describe the abiotic and biotic components of a pond.

An ecosystem is a unit of all the living organisms of an area together with their non-living surroundings, interacting with each other. Pond — abiotic: water, sunlight, temperature, dissolved oxygen and carbon dioxide, minerals, soil and stones at the bottom. Biotic: producers — phytoplankton, algae and rooted or floating plants such as Hydrilla and lotus; consumers — zooplankton and insect larvae (primary), small fish and frogs (secondary), large fish and birds (tertiary); decomposers — bacteria and fungi in the mud that break down dead matter.

Describe the role of adaptations with examples: (a) spongy stem of lotus (b) desert reptiles excrete uric acid (c) thick feathers of penguins (d) eyes on top of the head in aquatic animals. Also explain detritus and grazing food chains.

(a) Air spaces make the stem light and buoyant and it bends with currents. (b) Uric acid is excreted as a near-solid, saving water in the desert. (c) Densely packed feathers trap air and reduce heat loss in extreme cold. (d) The animal can stay hidden under water while watching for predators or prey above. Grazing chain: starts with green plants (grass → deer → tiger). Detritus chain: starts with dead organic matter (dead leaves → bacteria → earthworm → bird).
Compare the S-shaped and J-shaped population growth curves.

S-shaped (sigmoid): growth is slow at first (lag phase), then rapid (growth phase, births far exceed deaths), then levels off at the carrying capacity (stable phase) as environmental resistance makes births equal deaths. J-shaped: the population grows exponentially until environmental resistance suddenly takes effect, and then crashes as deaths rise sharply. The S curve shows gradual regulation; the J curve shows sudden collapse.
